They previously made an even bigger purchase of AU$471k worth of shares at a price of AU$0.84 per share. So it's clear an insider wanted to buy, even at a higher price than the current share price (being AU$0.69). It's very possible they regret the purchase, but it's more likely they are bullish about the company. To us, it's very important to consider the price insiders pay for shares. In the last twelve months insiders purchased 1.43m shares for AU$911k. But they sold 97.01k shares for AU$77k. Overall, Omega Oil & Gas insiders were net buyers during the last year. data.title: Why Rolls Royce Through ETFs Could Change The Risk You Carry
data.description:
You have a clear fork in the road with Rolls-Royce Holdings. You can own the stock directly and carry the company’s specific issues yourself, including Simply Wall St’s risk check that profit margins of 13.1% are lower than last year’s 29.6%, and its warning that weaker free cash flow could weigh on operating margins and earnings. Or you can own a fund that holds Rolls-Royce alongside many other businesses, which limits how much those company level swings hit your portfolio while also capping the upside.

Fresh news gives you a live example of how that trade off plays out. A new £8.7b defence contract for Babcock lifted the wider sector on 26 November 2026, and Rolls-Royce moved higher with it as aerospace and defence stocks climbed together. If you prefer to hold Rolls-Royce through a fund, WCMI, EWU and RCTR are three ETFs that include the company inside a broader mix of holdings.

Rather choose individual stocks than a fund? Explore 36 high quality undervalued stocks.

First Trust WCM International Equity ETF (WCMI)

WCMI gives Rolls-Royce Holdings real weight in your portfolio, with the stock at 6.27% and sitting as the second largest position. Each US$1,000 in the ETF translates to roughly US$63 in Rolls-Royce, so you are meaningfully tied to how the business performs. The rest of WCMI spreads across other areas. There is roughly 9.9% in aerospace and defense peers, 9.0% in diversified banks, 8.9% in semiconductors through companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, and further slices in pharmaceuticals, application software, casinos and gaming, consumer electronics and food retail.

Profit margins at Rolls-Royce Holdings are 13.1%, compared with 29.6% last year. That specific squeeze is cushioned in WCMI by holdings that depend on different drivers, such as Constellation Software in application software and large diversified banks tied to lending and financial services. Sector level shocks to aerospace and defense would still wash through the 9.9% allocation, so these positions spread where your risk comes from but do not remove the uncertainty around future Rolls-Royce profitability.

iShares MSCI United Kingdom ETF (EWU)

EWU spreads your money across large UK groups, with Rolls-Royce Holdings at 4.68% as the fourth biggest position. Each US$1,000 gives you about US$47 in Rolls-Royce, while more of your result comes from diversified banks at 18.1%, pharmaceuticals at 13.3% and integrated oil and gas at 12.7%. HSBC Holdings and Shell together account for 18.6% of the ETF, and AstraZeneca adds more healthcare weight. As a result, Rolls-Royce sits as one meaningful piece inside a broad UK equity mix.

One risk for Rolls-Royce Holdings is that higher investment or shifting demand reduces free cash flow and puts pressure on group operating margins and earnings. EWU’s exposure to banks, oil and gas and healthcare depends on different customer bases and cash flow patterns, which can dilute that company specific strain. You still rely heavily on how the wider UK market and large domestic sectors perform over time.

First Trust Bloomberg Nuclear Power ETF (RCTR)

Electric utilities such as Duke Energy and Southern set the tone in RCTR, and together with Talen Energy they pull a large slice of the fund toward power generation and grid infrastructure. Aerospace and defense holdings take 12.3%, where Rolls-Royce Holdings is one of several stocks in that pocket. The position is 4.39% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 in RCTR holds about US$44 in Rolls-Royce while most of your result rests on utilities, independent power producers and other industrial groups.

One risk for Rolls-Royce Holdings is that airlines, data center customers and governments slow their ordering, which would affect future revenue and operating profit. RCTR’s heavy exposure to electric utilities, coal producers and heavy electrical equipment depends more on electricity demand and infrastructure spending than on aircraft engines or data center projects, so the impact of weaker Rolls-Royce orders is partly absorbed by businesses tied to different customer decisions and capital cycles.

See what you'd actually own if you bought RCTR, from its 49 positions to how much sits in the top 10.

Choosing your Rolls-Royce fund exposure

You have three different ways to keep Rolls-Royce Holdings in your portfolio without owning the stock directly. WCMI puts the largest slice in the company at about US$63 per US$1,000 and spreads the rest across 49 other holdings worldwide, although you pay the highest fee at US$85 a year on US$10,000. EWU charges the least at US$50 on the same amount and owns the broadest mix with 75 stocks, but the company weight drops to roughly US$47 per US$1,000.

RCTR keeps Rolls-Royce near EWU’s stake at about US$44 per US$1,000, yet leans heavily on utilities and power producers. A day like the recent defence driven rally shows how all three can move with sector news, while the long term experience will differ based on whether you want a global mix, a UK heavy portfolio or a nuclear power themed ETF. One more factor to consider is that softer free cash flow at Rolls-Royce could influence each fund in line with how much it owns. Your choice is which mix and fee level fits the exposure you want to this business inside a larger portfolio.
